title: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds"
hookLine: the lord who raises and tends every world, not just yours
last: ALHAMDULILLAH — PRAISE, WHATEVER THE DAY DID.

cards: On day two you heard al-Fatiha whole, all seven verses in one go. For the next five days it slows down: one verse at a time, inside words you may have said a thousand times. Verse two begins with yesterday's word.
Praise be to God. Then it points that praise somewhere enormous. Not at your day.

teach.b: Verse two: “Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds.” In Arabic, al-hamdu lillahi rabbi l-'alamin. The first half is yesterday's word.
The new word is Rabb. English says Lord, which is right, but thin. Rabb is the one who owns and the one who looks after.
Commentators explain it with the picture of raising something: bringing a child, or a seedling, along step by step until it's grown. So a rabb isn't a distant owner with paperwork.
It's the one who feeds, shelters and brings you up.
Then al-'alamin: the worlds. Not the world: the worlds, plural. Commentators have listed people, angels, animals, every kind of created thing.
The ant colony under the sidewalk. The deep sea. The inside of a stranger's life on the train.
All of it, the verse says, is being raised and tended by one Rabb. And remember the conversation from day two.
At this verse, God answers: My servant has praised Me. The praise isn't said into empty air. It's heard, and answered.

how: Muslims say this verse in Arabic in every unit of every prayer, and many say alhamdulillah, its opening word, many times a day. Rabb is also the word Muslims use in many personal prayers, often as Rabbi, my Lord, or Rabbana, our Lord.

games.q: what's inside verse two — tap the pairs.
p: the one who owns, raises and tends
God's answer, in a hadith qudsi

s: it means lord and owner, and also the one who raises and looks after what's his.
the verse says Lord of the world, singular
al-'alamin is plural: the worlds, every kind of created thing.
the first words of verse two are yesterday's word, alhamdulillah
al-hamdu lillah: praise be to God.

games.q: someone praying says: praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds. in the hadith qudsi from day two, what happens next?
o: nothing: prayer is a one-way message.
God answers: My servant has praised Me.
games.why: the hadith describes al-Fatiha as a conversation. at this verse, God answers: My servant has praised Me.

practice: Sit comfortably. First, your own world: one thing in it that's being looked after, even today. Stay with it.
Then a world that isn't yours: a bird, a stranger, a field somewhere you'll never see. Then hold both at once. If you want, the Arabic can ride out on a breath: al-hamdu lillahi rabbi l-'alamin.

wordCard.voice: Rabb. Lord: the one who owns, raises and looks after, here the Lord of all the worlds. Twelfth word.

orig.note: Arabic: lord, master, the one who raises and looks after. in al-Fatiha: rabbi l-'alamin, Lord of the Worlds.

carryVoice: Your line: every world is tended. Yours, and every one you'll never see. Day twelve.

sources.q: Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 395 (the hadith qudsi of al-Fatiha as a conversation)
